title: Tool Design Best Practices
summary: A model can only use a tool as well as the tool is designed. Good tools have clear names and descriptions the model can reason about, the right granularity (not fifty overlapping tools, not one god-tool), safe side-effect behavior (idempotency, least privilege), and return concise, model-friendly output. Tool design is prompt engineering for actions — it decides whether the agent picks the right tool and calls it correctly.

subtopics.title: Name and describe tools the way the model reads them
subtopics.explanation: The model chooses tools purely from their names and descriptions, so those are prompt real estate, not documentation afterthoughts. A vague name like 'process' or a terse description forces the model to guess when to call it; a precise verb-noun name plus a one-line 'use this when...' description makes selection reliable. How you word a tool is the single biggest lever on whether the model picks the right one.

subtopics.title: Get the granularity right
subtopics.explanation: Too many narrow tools overwhelm the model's selection and bloat the prompt; one broad 'do everything' tool pushes all the hard decisions into free-text arguments the model gets wrong. The sweet spot is a small set of tools that each map to one clear intent with a stable interface. Right-sized granularity keeps the model's choice space small enough to reason about while still covering the task.
subtopics.example:
# too granular: 4 tools that are really one intent
# get_order_total, get_order_date, get_order_items, get_order_status

# too broad: everything crammed into a free-text command
{"name": "db", "description": "Run any operation.",
 "parameters": {"command": {"type": "string"}}}  # model must invent SQL

# right: one intent, structured args
{"name": "get_order", "parameters": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}}}

subtopics.title: Make tools idempotent and side-effect safe
subtopics.explanation: Agents retry, loop, and sometimes call the same tool twice, so any tool with side effects should be safe to repeat — creating a resource with a client-supplied idempotency key, or checking-then-acting so a duplicate call is a no-op. A read tool is naturally safe; a 'charge card' or 'send email' tool is dangerous if a retry doubles it. Designing for repeat calls is what makes an agent's inherent retrying safe rather than catastrophic.

subtopics.title: Grant least privilege
subtopics.explanation: A tool should expose the narrowest capability that gets the job done — scoped, read-only where possible, and never a raw shell or unrestricted database handle. Broad tools turn a model mistake or prompt injection into real damage, while narrow tools cap the blast radius. Least privilege is the security boundary that keeps a hallucinated or manipulated tool call from becoming a breach.

subtopics.title: Return concise, model-friendly output
subtopics.explanation: Tool output goes straight back into the prompt as tokens, so a tool that dumps a 5,000-row JSON blob wastes context, buries the signal, and confuses the model. Return only the fields the model needs, summarized or paginated, in a stable shape. Concise output is both a cost lever and an accuracy lever — the model reasons better over a tight result than a firehose.

foundations.overview: Tool design is prompt engineering aimed at actions: the model decides which tool to call and what arguments to pass using nothing but the tool's name, description, and parameter schema, then reasons over whatever the tool returns. Five principles make tools work well with a model. Names and descriptions must read like instructions — a precise verb-noun name and a 'use this when...' description drive correct selection. Granularity must be balanced — a small set of single-intent tools beats both a swarm of overlapping ones and a single god-tool that hides decisions in free text. Side-effecting tools must be idempotent and safe to repeat, because agents retry and loop. Every tool should follow least privilege, exposing the narrowest capability rather than a raw shell or open SQL, so a mistake or injection has a small blast radius. And output must be concise and model-friendly, since results become prompt tokens that cost money and shape accuracy. Treating tool design with the same care as prompt design is what makes the difference between an agent that reliably picks and uses the right tool and one that flails.
foundations.formalDefinition: Tool design is the practice of specifying an agent's tools — their names, descriptions, parameter schemas, granularity, side-effect semantics, permission scope, and output shape — so that an LLM can reliably select the correct tool, supply valid arguments, safely repeat calls, and reason over concise results.
foundations.whyItMatters: The model can only be as effective as its tools allow: poor names cause wrong-tool selection, over-broad tools cause invalid calls and security risk, non-idempotent side effects turn normal retries into duplicated damage, and verbose output inflates cost and degrades reasoning. Good tool design is therefore one of the highest-leverage, lowest-cost ways to raise an agent's reliability and safety.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of tools as the buttons on a control panel you hand a capable but literal operator who can only read the labels. Clear, well-labeled buttons for exactly the actions needed get pressed correctly; a panel with fifty cryptic buttons, or one giant button wired to everything, gets misused — and any button that does something dangerous had better be safe to press twice.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding agents exposing scoped read_file / run_tests tools rather than a raw shell, support agents given a specific issue_refund tool with an idempotency key, research agents with a single well-described search tool that returns capped summaries, and data agents given parameterized read queries instead of arbitrary SQL.
commonUseCases: Writing tool names/descriptions the model selects correctly
Choosing single-intent tools over god-tools or tool sprawl
Adding idempotency keys to side-effecting tools
Scoping tools to least privilege and capping output size

commonMisconceptions.myth: Descriptions are just documentation for developers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model reads the name and description to decide when to call a tool — they are part of the prompt and are the biggest lever on correct tool selection.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More tools make the agent more capable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Too many overlapping tools bloat the prompt and confuse selection. A small set of clear, single-intent tools usually outperforms a large sprawling one.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Idempotency only matters for humans clicking twice.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Agents retry and loop by design, so a non-idempotent side-effecting tool (charge, send, create) can double up on a single automatic retry — idempotency is essential, not optional.

interactiveWidget.title: The tool-design checklist
interactiveWidget.caption: A quick mental pass to run over every tool you expose to an agent before you ship it.

config.note: Before exposing a tool, check five things. NAME & DESCRIPTION: is the name a clear verb-noun (search_orders, not handle), and does the description say WHEN to use it? GRANULARITY: does it map to one intent — not four near-duplicates, not a god-tool that hides decisions in free text? SIDE-EFFECT SAFETY: if it changes state (charge, send, create), is it idempotent so an automatic retry can't double it? LEAST PRIVILEGE: does it expose the narrowest capability (a scoped read), not a raw shell or open SQL? OUTPUT: is the return small, stable, and only the fields the model needs — since every returned token costs money and competes for the model's attention? If a tool fails any of these, the model will either pick it wrong, call it wrong, or make it do damage. Tool design is prompt engineering for actions: spend the same care on it as you spend on the system prompt.

checkpoints.prompt: What does the model actually use to decide whether to call a given tool?
options: The tool's name and description (and parameter schema)
How fast the tool ran last time
checkpoints.explanation: The model only sees each tool's name, description, and parameter schema. Those are effectively part of the prompt, which is why a clear verb-noun name and a 'use this when...' description are the biggest lever on correct tool selection.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is idempotency especially important for an agent's side-effecting tools?
options: It makes the tool run faster
Because agents retry and loop, so a non-idempotent tool can duplicate a charge/email on an automatic retry
It reduces the size of the response
It is required by JSON Schema
checkpoints.explanation: Agents retry transient failures and may re-enter the loop, so a non-idempotent tool like charge_card or send_email can fire twice on a single automatic retry. An idempotency key makes a repeated call a safe no-op.

checkpoints.prompt: A search tool returns this. Why is it a poor result to hand back to the model?
checkpoints.code:
def search(q):
    rows = db.query(q)          # returns 4000 rows
    return rows                  # every row, every column, as JSON

result = search("orders")
print(len(json.dumps(result)))   # e.g. 812_450
options: It's fine — more context always helps the model
It dumps thousands of rows straight into the prompt as tokens, wasting context and cost and burying the signal the model needs
checkpoints.explanation: Tool output becomes prompt tokens, so returning a huge blob wastes context, inflates cost, and buries the useful fields. Return only what the model needs — cap, summarize, or paginate — in a small, stable shape.

keyTakeaways: Tool names and descriptions are prompt real estate — clear verb-noun names plus 'use this when...' descriptions drive correct tool selection.
Aim for a small set of single-intent tools; avoid both tool sprawl and a god-tool that hides decisions in free-text arguments.
Make side-effecting tools idempotent (e.g. idempotency keys) so the agent's built-in retrying can't double a charge, email, or record.
Follow least privilege: expose the narrowest, scoped capability instead of a raw shell or open SQL to cap the blast radius of a bad call.
Return concise, stable, model-friendly output — every returned token costs money and competes for the model's attention.
